Two weeks have passed since the EMP separated us from the rest of the world, and in that time we've heard nothing. No new planes, no radio signals, no ships; not a single electronic sausage. The only potential communication system on the island has grey feathers and smells of pigeon shit.

The inhabitants of the island have pulled together, balancing their time judiciously between discussing matters in the pub, seeing to essential tasks, and generally taking a bit of a holiday from all the things that require electricity and internet. Sandra has been organizing meals at the local pub, and has worked out a basic barter system based on units of alcohol, and the pub's ancient juke box had been replaced with a nightly open mic. Gambling abounds, and a new dartboard has been installed! The passengers of Ryanair's last inbound flight are enjoying their unusual holiday experience, and are planning to charge back their accommodation when they get off this weird little island that doesn't take any of their credit cards. In the meantime they are enjoying what can only be an iron-clad excuse for getting out of work. Various drunken holiday liasons have occurred, and there are a few people avoiding each other's gaze in the pub.

No one has made any serious efforts to figure out what's going on - after all, we live on an island, it's only been two weeks; there's a fair chance that if we just hang on for another week it'll all be fine. Maybe we had too much of Abe's wine!

Then a stormy night falls, and a red dawn rises, tinting the sea with shades of orange and pink.

Red sky in the morning... no sane farmer ignores that. A storm is coming. Storms don't take their time to call on these islands; usually you have an early warning system. Today, all you get is the ominous red sun. We've probably got about four hours till it hits us, according to the farmers now running out of the pub and shouting for volunteers to help.

With no way to call for aid, and no new supplies in sight, the island's livestock and crops could be essential to our survival.

It's time to harvest most of the early summer fruits we'll need to bottle for the winter, and the island's fruit trees have just put out fresh buds. The cows are calving, the sheep are lambing, the goats are having kids and the chickens are broody and it's not good to freak out a broody hen. Half the village just planted up their vegetable gardens. In the fields, the early wheat turns a perfect shade of gold.

Before this day is over, anything not in a barn, covered safely, or harvested and home is going to get ripped to shreds by gale-force winds or blown straight off the edge of a cliff.
